chunks: "The ISA is the contract between software and hardware. It defines what instructions exist, how many registers there are, how memory is addressed and what happens on an exception.
If I compile a program for an ISA, that binary has to run on any chip that implements it.

The microarchitecture is how a particular chip actually delivers that contract: how deep the pipeline is, how many instructions it issues per cycle, whether it executes out of order, how big the caches are, what branch predictor it uses.
The classic example is x86. An Intel core and an AMD core run the same binaries, but inside they're completely different designs.
Same with Arm: a tiny in-order Cortex-M and a wide out-of-order Cortex-A both implement an Arm ISA, one for a microcontroller and one for a phone.
The reason the split matters is that it lets hardware change without breaking software.
A new generation can be wider, faster and use a new predictor, and every old program still works.
The ISA is stable and the microarchitecture is where the performance and power are won.
The one caveat is that while microarchitecture is invisible to correct programs, it's not invisible to timing, which is why cache and speculation side channels exist."
